Senses.Explanation: Literally, “awaken through-and-through.” The term appears 142 times in 71 allowlisted texts, both as a verb in encounter and biographical retrospectives and as a noun-like condition in instruction and contrast. Wuyi Yuanlai supplies the clearest corpus definition: there are two awakenings, “interpretive awakening obtained from written words and speech” and “thorough awakening obtained by investigating on one’s own part”; he adds, “interpretive awakening is like hearing someone describe a thing; thorough awakening is like seeing the thing with one’s own eyes” (解悟者如聞人說物，徹悟者如親眼見物). Other records say not to stop if one has not thoroughly awakened, describe the World-honored One seeing the morning star and thoroughly awakening, and contrast the many who thoroughly awaken with the equally many who misunderstand. Thus the Chan record bends an ordinary intensive verb into a named contrast with “interpretive awakening” (解悟), while also using it in lineage biographies; the direct contrast, not an imported theory of enlightenment, controls the gloss.
Senses.Note: Verbal and noun-like grammar denotes the same event/state and does not warrant a split. The related term “interpretive awakening” (解悟) is a text-drawn contrast, not an annotator’s ranking.
